_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications.
rashi:a1.1: Mishna. All those forbidden [for the altar] prohibit in any amount: even if one was intermingled with a thousand, they are all forbidden for the altar, if it cannot be recognized. All of them can be found in a case where they cannot be recognized; but a tereifa can be found so only as it is explained in tractate Zevaḥim, in the chapter Kol HaZevaḥim SheNitarevu (Zevaḥim 74b): for example, an animal mauled by a wolf that was intermingled with one pierced by a thorn; or alternatively, with the offspring of a tereifa, according to Rabbi Eliezer, who says it may not be sacrificed.
tosafot:a1.1: Mishna: All those forbidden. [A heading only.]
gershom:a1.1: They prohibit for the altar in any amount: they prohibit all the animals with which they were intermingled, even if those are ten thousand.
gershom:a2.1: And the tereifa: for example, where the gullet was pierced and afterward the [skin] healed over it, and afterward it was intermingled with others. [A note in the printed edition asks why Rabbeinu does not explain as the Gemara does in Zevaḥim 74b, cited by Rashi here, since by his explanation the animal would be called a carcass and not a tereifa; it leaves this to be settled.]
gershom:a3.1: With sin offerings left to die: those five sin offerings that are left to die.
rashi:a4.1: Gemara. And it was difficult for us: there, what is the “even” that it says? For it teaches: “All the offerings that were intermingled with sin offerings left to die,” which implies that one of the offerings was intermingled with many sin offerings left to die, and even one permitted animal in ten thousand forbidden ones, they all die. What is it saying? It is obvious to us; all the more so, when the forbidden are more numerous it is obvious that they die, since the forbidden are the majority.
gershom:a4.1: And it was difficult for us, what is it saying? It is obvious that when one offering was intermingled with sin offerings left to die, they all die, since most of them are left to die.
rashi:a5.1: And we answered: there, this is what it teaches: “All the offerings with which one of the sin offerings left to die was intermingled,” implying that one sin offering was intermingled among the offerings when they were many; and even one forbidden animal in ten thousand permitted ones, they all die, and the one is not nullified among them. So why do I need to go back and teach it here?
gershom:a5.1: Rather, this is what it says: All the fit offerings with which one of the sin offerings left to die was intermingled, even one in ten thousand, they all die, since it is not nullified by a majority.
rashi:a6.1: There it is: with regard to sin offerings left to die and an ox to be stoned.
rashi:a6.2: That they are items forbidden for benefit: and for that reason they are significant and are not nullified.
rashi:a6.3: But: these of our mishna, an animal that copulated with a person and an animal that was the object of bestiality, which are permitted to an ordinary person for eating. For we are dealing here with a case where it copulated or was the object of bestiality on the basis of one witness, so that it is not stoned on that account, or where the owners admitted it, and one who admits to [an act that carries] a fine is exempt. Say: let them be nullified. Our mishna teaches us [otherwise]. And in Zevaḥim we read further: and had it taught us that of Temurah, I would say it is here, since they are repulsive to the Most High, that they are not nullified, and they graze until they become blemished and an ordinary person eats them; but a thing forbidden to an ordinary person too, say it is nullified. It teaches us there: they die. For even with regard to an ordinary person it is not nullified, since if it were nullified, let it say: they graze until they become blemished, are redeemed, and an ordinary person eats them.
tosafot:a6.1: But here, where they are not [items forbidden for] benefit, say: let them be nullified by a majority. And in the chapter HaTa’arovet (Zevaḥim 71b) it says: and had it taught us only here, I would say that they are permitted to an ordinary person; it teaches us the one taught there, “they shall die,” and they are forbidden even to an ordinary person.
gershom:a6.1: That applies to something forbidden for benefit: for these five sin offerings and the ox to be stoned are forbidden for benefit.
gershom:a7.1: But when something not forbidden for benefit is intermingled, such as those of our mishna, the prostitute’s payment, the price of a dog, the diverse kinds and the tereifa: for that our mishna was needed.
tosafot:a7.1: And the animal that copulated with a person and the one that was the object of bestiality: there, in the chapter HaTa’arovet (ibid.), it answers: from there, does it teach in what proportion? Here it teaches “in any amount.” And the one there was needed to teach us the remedy. (And here it answers them in another way.)
gershom:a8.1: And this too we learned, in the latter clause of that [mishna], “All the offerings with which an animal that copulated or was the object of bestiality was intermingled”: it speaks of an animal that copulated on the basis of one witness or on the basis of the owners, which is not liable to death and is not forbidden for benefit.
rashi:a7.1: We learn there in Zevaḥim, [regarding] an animal that copulated: one of the offerings that was intermingled with a non-sacred animal that copulated with a person or was the object of bestiality: they graze until they become blemished and are sold, and he brings an offering of that same kind with the money of the best among them. That is, of the kind of the offering that was intermingled with them: if it was a peace offering, he brings a peace offering with the money of the best of them, since the hand of the Temple treasury is uppermost; and if it was a burnt offering, he brings a burnt offering with the money of the best. Evidently we learn from there that they are not nullified by a majority.
gershom:a9.1: They are all sold, and he brings with the money of the best of them one of that same kind: that is, if they were intermingled with burnt offerings, a guilt offering, peace offerings or a sin offering, they are sold, and he brings with the money of the best [an offering] of that kind, to discharge his obligation; but they themselves are not sacrificed. Even though an animal that copulated or was the object of bestiality is not forbidden for benefit: evidently, though they are not forbidden for benefit, they are not nullified by a majority. [Rendered with the correction the printed edition suggests.]
rashi:a8.1: One with non-sacred: the mishna here deals with where they were intermingled while non-sacred, and afterward he consecrated them; and the one in Zevaḥim deals with where they were intermingled when they were sacred, for there it teaches “All the offerings.”
gershom:a10.1: And Rav Shimi said to me: that is why it was necessary to state it here and there, for one is with non-sacred animals: the mishna here deals [with where they were intermingled with non-sacred animals, and the one of “All the offerings” deals] with where they were intermingled with sacred animals. And both are necessary: for had it taught us about sacred animals, [I would say] that is why they are not nullified, because an animal that copulated or was the object of bestiality is repulsive to be made sacred; but with non-sacred animals, let them be nullified. For that our mishna was needed.
rashi:a9.1: But: here, with non-sacred animals, which are not repulsive at the time of mixing, since the share of the Most High has no bearing on them, say they are nullified; and when he consecrates them they are properly sanctified, since the prohibition has already been nullified, and they may be sacrificed. It teaches us [otherwise]. And in Zevaḥim it asks: let it teach this one of Temurah, and that one of Zevaḥim would not be needed. And it answers: here [in Zevaḥim] the remedy was needed, which is why he taught it again here in Zevaḥim. For there in Temurah he taught “they prohibit in any amount” and did not teach the remedy, and here he taught the remedy: they are sold, and he brings with the money of the best of them one of that same kind.
gershom:a13.1: Another version: had it been [only] from that one, “an animal that copulated or was the object of bestiality was intermingled with them,” I would have said that applies only to sacred animals.
gershom:a14.1: But with non-sacred: [if] they were intermingled with non-sacred animals, say it is not forbidden but they are nullified. This mishna teaches us, since it deals with where they were intermingled with non-sacred animals, that they are not nullified.
rashi:a10.1: And with non-sacred too we learn: that even with actual non-sacred items, living animals and all these that are significant are not nullified by a majority.
gershom:a11.1: And with non-sacred too we learned: “And these are forbidden and prohibit in any amount: libation wine…,” that they are not nullified with non-sacred items either. Even so, our mishna is needed for them, for from there I would have said: this is the reason they are not nullified in a majority of non-sacred items, because all of these, libation wine and the rest, are forbidden for benefit; but here, let them be nullified, since they are not forbidden for benefit. That is why our mishna was needed: they are not nullified.
rashi:a10.2: And hides with a tear opposite the heart [levuvin]: it is explained in tractate Avoda Zara (32a) that they pierce a round hole opposite the heart, and through that hole they took out the sacrificial portions and burned them for idol worship; and an offering to idol worship is forbidden for benefit.
rashi:a11.1: And the hair of a nazirite: it is forbidden for benefit, since it must be put under the pot [Numbers 6:18].
rashi:a11.2: And meat in milk: a piece of meat that was cooked in milk and was then intermingled with a thousand pieces; they are all forbidden. This follows the one who says that meat in milk is forbidden for benefit, in Sheḥitat Ḥullin, in the chapter Kol HaBasar (Ḥullin 114b).
rashi:a12.1: What is different there: with sacrificial animals, where he teaches items forbidden for benefit, such as sin offerings left to die and an ox to be stoned, together with items forbidden for eating, such as a tereifa?
rashi:a12.2: A mixture of non-sacred items, etc.: that is, in tractate Avoda Zara, with a mixture of non-sacred items, he broke off and taught items forbidden for benefit alone, as he teaches: “And these are forbidden and prohibit in any amount, and are forbidden for benefit: libation wine…,” and then teaches in a separate list: “And these are things that are not forbidden for benefit: milk that a gentile milked without a Jew watching him…” It stands to reason: he is in tractate Avoda Zara, and he wants to explain prohibitions that resemble libation wine, that they too are forbidden for benefit. Here too, with offerings, [he lists] those that resemble them, since all of them are forbidden to the Most High.
gershom:a15.1: And items forbidden for benefit, such as the set-aside and the worshipped animal, which are not nullified among non-sacred animals: why was it necessary to teach them in our mishna? He already taught it once, as we learned: “These are forbidden and prohibit in any amount: libation wine, an object of idol worship and hides with a tear opposite the heart,” that they are not nullified among non-sacred items. From that I would have said: that applies only to those prohibitions forbidden for benefit, like these, all of which are forbidden for benefit, that when intermingled with non-sacred items they are not nullified; but prohibitions not forbidden for benefit, such as the prostitute’s payment, the price of a dog, diverse kinds and the tereifa, when intermingled with non-sacred animals, say they are nullified. That is why our mishna was needed: [to teach] that they are not.
gershom:a12.1: And had it taught us only this mishna, I would have said: this is the reason they are not nullified among these non-sacred animals, because they are wanted for the Most High and are repulsive; [but] for an ordinary person, say even items forbidden for benefit are nullified by a majority. That is why “And these are forbidden…” was needed: that even for an ordinary person they are not nullified.
gershom:a16.1: And what is different with regard to being intermingled with sacred animals? This mishna, and the mishna “All the offerings with which were intermingled…,” there too teaches the tereifa with them, which is forbidden for eating. For it teaches a prohibition of benefit and a prohibition of eating together: the set-aside and the worshipped animal are prohibitions of benefit, while the tereifa is forbidden not for benefit but only for eating, and he teaches them together.
gershom:a17.1: And with a mixture of non-sacred items he broke off and taught prohibitions of benefit alone: such as libation wine, an object of idol worship and hides with a tear opposite the heart.
gershom:a18.1: And a prohibition of eating alone: for it teaches in the latter clause, “And these are forbidden for eating and permitted for benefit: milk that a gentile milked without a Jew watching him…” [This is the reason: when he is in tractate Avoda Zara, since he wants to explain the prohibition of libation wine, he explains the prohibitions that resemble it. When he is in our mishna, since he wants to explain the set-aside, the worshipped animal, the prostitute’s payment and the price of a dog, which are forbidden for the altar, he explains also everything forbidden for the altar, even a prohibition…] [A note in the printed edition: that mishna, “These are forbidden for eating,” is in the second chapter [of Avoda Zara] and is not a latter clause at all, and the Gemara there (74a) gives the reason; Rabbeinu’s words require study.]
rashi:a14.1: From the cattle: implying, and not all the cattle.
rashi:a15.1: But isn’t it logical: and no verse is needed.
rashi:a16.1: Plowing with an ox and a donkey shall prove: for it is permitted to the Most High if one consecrated it afterward.
tosafot:a16.1: Plowing with an ox and a donkey shall prove, with which a transgression was committed and which is permitted for the altar: as we expound: “of any of these” [Leviticus 22:25] you may not sacrifice, but you may sacrifice sacrificial animals with which a transgression was committed.
rashi:a18.1: Take back what you brought: for it is not a refutation, for this reason [that plowing does not carry the death penalty].
rashi:a18.2: Here is a case where a transgression was committed with them before two witnesses: that is, you may derive by this inference the animal about which two witnesses testify that it copulated or was the object of bestiality, since it is certainly liable to death and forbidden to the Most High.
tosafot:a18.1: Take back what you brought: Rashi explained: it is not a refutation, for this reason. Here is a case where a transgression was committed with it before two witnesses: that is, you may derive by this inference the animal about which two witnesses testify that it copulated or was the object of bestiality, since it is certainly liable to death and forbidden to the Most High. On the basis of one witness or of the owners, where there is no death penalty, from where would you know that they are forbidden to the Most High, were it not for the verse? End of his words. And if you will say: why do I need an a fortiori inference for an animal that copulated or was the object of bestiality on the basis of two witnesses? Derive it from “from the well-watered pastures of Israel” below (Temurah 29a), where we expound: from what is permitted to Israel; and this one is forbidden for benefit. One can say: it is needed where one slaughtered and sacrificed it before its sentence was concluded, when it is permitted for benefit, as stated in Bava Kamma, chapter Arba’a VeḤamisha (41a). Alternatively, one can explain “take back what you brought”: here is a case where a transgression was committed with it before two witnesses, and I do not even need the a fortiori inference, since even without it one knows that it is forbidden for the altar.
gershom:a19.1: Take back what you brought: that is, take an answer from the proof you brought. Here is a case where a transgression was committed with them before two witnesses: that is, from this inference we learned [the case] where a transgression was committed with them before two witnesses; an animal that copulated or was the object of bestiality on the testimony of one witness we did not learn. That is why “from the cattle” was needed, to exclude them. For Rabbi (Yishmael) [Shimon] said: I infer an animal that copulated or was the object of bestiality on one witness by an a fortiori inference: “And if a blemished animal…”
rashi:a19.1: On the basis of one witness or on the basis of the owners: where there is no death penalty, from where would you know that it is forbidden to the Most High, were it not for the verse?
rashi:a20.1: I infer it: and no verse is needed.
rashi:a20.2: The admission of one witness disqualifies it from sacrifice: for once a Sage has said that it is a permanent blemish, it is disqualified from sacrifice.
rashi:a20.3: Disqualifies it from eating: for it is [subject to] stoning.
gershom:a20.1: The admission of one witness disqualifies it from sacrifice: as we said in the chapter Kol Pesulei HaMukdashin: an Israelite is deemed credible to say, “I gave this firstborn to a priest in its blemished state.”
gershom:a21.1: An animal that copulated or was the object of bestiality: two witnesses disqualify it from eating, since it is liable to death; is it not logical that one witness disqualifies it from sacrifice? The verse states: “From the cattle.” So why do I need a verse for an animal that copulated or was the object of bestiality on the testimony of one witness?
gershom:a22.1: But this is derived by inference, as Rabbi Yishmael [the daf has Rabbi Shimon] said, that it can be learned by inference. Rav Ashi said: it was needed, since one can say there is a refutation at the basis of the inference: what about a blemished animal, whose blemish is conspicuous to everyone? Will you say…
tosafot:b1.1: Rav Ashi said: Because one can say that the refutation is in the basis of the inference, etc.: in the Torat Kohanim [Sifra], Rabbi Akiva says this refutation to him: what about a blemished animal, whose blemish is revealed? And that is what it says here, “whose blemish is conspicuous.” It is puzzling: why does he not say, a prostitute’s payment and the price of a dog shall prove, whose blemish is not conspicuous and which are forbidden for the altar?
rashi:b3.1: Their coatings: if one covered it with something after they gave it to her, the coating is permitted to come into the Temple, to make plates for the altar; for the Torah forbade only “even both of them,” and not their coatings.
rashi:b3.2: A worshipped animal, whose coatings are forbidden: as it is written: “You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them…”
rashi:b3.3: A worshipped animal, which was made into an object of idol worship, is it not logical that it is itself forbidden to the Most High? Granted that it does not become forbidden to an ordinary person, since living creatures do not become forbidden, as we will give the reason below; but to the Most High at least it is forbidden, since its coatings are forbidden even for benefit to an ordinary person. So why do I need a verse?
tosafot:b3.1: And if a prostitute’s payment and the price of a dog, whose coatings are permitted: he could equally have made [another] a fortiori inference, as stated in the chapter Kol HaTzelamim (Avoda Zara 46b): and if a prostitute’s payment and the price of a dog, which are permitted to an ordinary person in what is detached, are forbidden to the Most High as living creatures, then a worshipped animal, which is forbidden to an ordinary person in what is detached, is it not logical that it is forbidden to the Most High as a living creature? And then one could not say “or reverse it,” as is said here. And in the chapter Kol HaTzelamim he did not make such an a fortiori inference to forbid the stones of a mountain for the altar, for it says there: and if a prostitute’s payment, which is permitted to an ordinary person in what is detached, is forbidden to the Most High in what is attached [to the ground], a worshipped object…; or reverse it: and if a prostitute’s payment and the price of a dog, which are forbidden, have their coatings permitted. And he could have made this a fortiori inference there, to permit the coating of a mountain, even for the altar.
gershom:b1.1: And if a prostitute’s payment and the price of a dog, whose coating is permitted: if one plated them with a covering of silver or gold, their coating is permitted, and they themselves are forbidden.
gershom:b2.1: A worshipped animal, whose coating is forbidden: “You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them…”
rashi:b4.1: Or reverse it: were the verse not written, one could reverse the law.
rashi:b4.2: A worshipped animal, which is permitted: for we have not found that it is forbidden.
tosafot:b4.1: Or reverse it, etc.: and if you will say: why does he not say that wherever one can argue toward leniency and toward stringency, we argue toward stringency? So it says in the chapter Kol HaTzelamim (Avoda Zara 46b). One can say: with living creatures we should rather argue toward leniency, since we should not forbid living creatures, given that an a fortiori inference toward leniency can be made.
tosafot:b4.2: A worshipped animal, which is permitted, is it not logical that its coating should be permitted: in the chapter HaShoḥet (Ḥullin 40a) it says that an offering to idol worship from a worshipped living creature is forbidden, for it says: this is where he said “to the mountain,” that is where he said “to the guardian spirit of the mountain,” whose offering is forbidden. Evidently we are more stringent with an offering of living creatures than with a coating. Yet with regard to a mountain it says the reverse: the coating of a mountain is forbidden, as stated in the chapter Kol HaTzelamim (Avoda Zara 45a), and its offering is permitted, as it says in the chapter HaShoḥet (Ḥullin 40a), “this is where he said to the mountain,” meaning that if he slaughtered for the sake of the mountain, its offering is permitted. One can say: what it says there, that the coating of a mountain is forbidden, means the coating that was on it at the time of the bowing down, and so too the coating of living creatures is then forbidden; what it says here, that it is permitted, refers to a coating that came after the bowing down. Alternatively, according to the conclusion here, that the coating of a worshipped animal is forbidden, it is well.
gershom:b3.1: Is it not logical that it is forbidden for the altar? Or reverse it: that is, I say the matter is reversed, to permit. And if a prostitute’s payment and the price of a dog, which are forbidden explicitly by the Torah, have their coating permitted, then a worshipped animal, which is permitted for the altar, since we have not found it explicitly forbidden by the Torah, is it not logical that its coating is permitted?
rashi:b5.1: This is what it says: if so, you have nullified “You shall not covet…” Therefore one cannot say “or reverse it”; and since it follows from the inference that a worshipped animal is forbidden to the Most High, the verse he cited is not needed.
gershom:b4.1: The first disputant said to him: if so, according to your words, that you wish to permit the coating of a worshipped animal, you have nullified “You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them…”
rashi:b6.1: I will establish it, etc.: therefore one can say “or reverse it”; and since it is permitted even to the Most High, its coatings are permitted.
gershom:b5.1: He said to you: I will establish it with regard to an entity that has no breath of life. That is, a worshipped entity with no breath of life: its coating is forbidden; but a worshipped entity with the breath of life, such as an animal, since it is permitted, as we said, let its coating be permitted. That is why “from the herd” was needed, to exclude the worshipped animal. This other version, “say, we found…,” my teacher did not tell us.
rashi:b6.2: The verse states “from the herd,” and not all the herd, to exclude the worshipped animal: that it is forbidden to the Most High; and since it is forbidden to the Most High, its coatings are forbidden even to an ordinary person, for we apply to it “You shall not covet…”
tosafot:b6.1: The verse states “from the herd,” to exclude the worshipped animal: Rashi explained: that it is forbidden to the Most High, and since it is forbidden to the Most High, its coating is forbidden even to an ordinary person, for we apply to it “the silver or the gold that is on them.” These are Rashi’s words. And he was right to explain it so. For one cannot say that even according to this exclusion the coating is permitted to an ordinary person, and that we establish “you shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them” for what has no breath of life, while with living creatures it is permitted to the Most High. For since it asks just below, “the reason is that the verse excluded it,” it implies that it is obvious to him that once the verse excluded it, every coating of a worshipped living creature is forbidden. And so the passage implies.
gershom:b9.1: But isn’t it written: “And you shall destroy their name”: everything made for their sake.
rashi:b8.1: Beit galya: a term of height. (Another version:) beit kalya, like kelua, destruction. Another version: beit karya, a privy, from the term “they dug [karu] a pit” (Jeremiah 18).
gershom:b10.1: This “and you shall destroy their name” comes only to obligate [us]
gershom:b11.1: to give them a derogatory name, as idol worship that is called Beit Galya: that is, revealed and known to all.
gershom:b12.1: One calls it Beit Kalya: that is, for their eyes to be consumed. [Rabbeinu Gershom reads beit kalya, where our text has beit karya.]
rashi:b10.1: From the context of the verse: for we find that with regard to bestiality the verse uses “animal” [behema], and with regard to a matter of idol worship it uses the term “herd” [bakar].
rashi:b11.1: Set-aside: which they set aside for use as an offering to idol worship.
rashi:b11.2: The one that gored: that killed a person, on the testimony of one witness, so that it is not stoned.
rashi:b11.3: If it is stated that it copulated: that it is forbidden for sacrifice. For aren’t both equal? If there were two witnesses to the matter, both are stoned.
gershom:b6.1: If it stated an animal that gored, why was it necessary to exclude one that copulated? Are not both [subject to] death, so let one be learned from the other? Because there is…
rashi:b12.1: One that gored: [the Torah] did not make forced like willing with regard to stoning, as we learned (Bava Kamma 39a): a stadium ox is not liable to stoning, as it is stated: “If an ox gore,” and not that others make it gore.
gershom:b7.1: That with an animal that copulated they made the forced like the willing: for if [a person] copulated with an animal by force, it is liable to death as if it were willing; which is not so with one that gored, as we learned: a stadium ox is not liable to death, as it is stated, “if an ox gore,” and not that others make it gore.
rashi:b13.1: Pays the ransom for it: even though the ox is stoned.
gershom:b8.1: It pays the ransom after [the ox’s] death, as it is written: “The ox shall be stoned… If a ransom be laid on him…” And this belongs above: “The reason is that the verse excluded it, ‘from the herd,’ to exclude the worshipped animal; but if not, the coating would be permitted.”
rashi:b14.1: And this tanna derives it from here: that an animal that copulated with a person and one that was the object of bestiality are forbidden to the Most High.
tosafot:b14.1: And this tanna derives it from here, as it is taught, etc.: it is puzzling, for here it implies that Rabbi Shimon does not hold this exposition of “because their corruption is in them,” since above he derives it from another verse, as he says: “If it is stated that it gored, why is it stated that it copulated?”, implying that he expounds it from “from the herd.” Yet in the chapter Ein Ma’amidin (Avoda Zara 23b) Rabbi Shimon says with regard to bestiality that it is disqualified, as it is written: “because their corruption is in them, there is a blemish in them,” evidently implying that he expounds it from “their corruption.” One can say: what he says above for Rabbi Shimon, “If it is stated that it gored,” he says to him according to the words of the first tanna, who derives it from “from the herd”; but he himself does not hold so, for he expounds it from “because their corruption.”
gershom:b13.1: [With regard to a domesticated animal [behema] it is written: “Neither shall any woman stand before an animal to lie down with it” [Leviticus 18:23]; therefore it stands to reason that “from the cattle” [behema] comes to exclude the animal that was the object of bestiality, and “herd” to exclude the worshipped animal, as it is written: “Thus they exchanged their glory for the likeness of an ox,” which is herd.] (Until here it belongs above.) And this tanna excludes them from here: the one that was the object of bestiality, the set-aside and the worshipped animal…
rashi:b14.2: “An animal with an extended limb and one with uncloven hooves”: we do not read [these words in this baraita].
gershom:b14.1: As the Sages taught: the one that was the object of bestiality and the set-aside, etc.: if he consecrated them, they are like sacrificial animals whose temporary blemish preceded their consecration, since none of these is written among the blemishes; and they need a permanent blemish to be redeemed, like the law of sacrificial animals whose temporary blemish preceded their consecration.
rashi:b16.1: That they are forbidden: for sacrifice.
gershom:b15.1: And from where that they are forbidden for the altar? As it is written: “because their corruption,” and the Master said, etc.: the one that was the object of bestiality, the set-aside and the worshipped animal are excluded by “corruption,” [which means] sexual immorality and idol worship. And the prostitute’s payment and the price of a dog are written explicitly in verses as forbidden for the altar.
rashi:b16.2: An animal that copulated with a person and one that was the object of bestiality: a matter of sexual immorality. The set-aside and the worshipped animal: a matter of idol worship.
tosafot:b17.1: Any case in which a blemish disqualifies, sexual immorality and idol worship disqualify: this requires study. What is it saying? We have properly expounded the animal that copulated and the one that was the object of bestiality from “because their corruption.”
gershom:b16.1: And where a blemish does not disqualify, such as with birds: he does not understand [these] from what the Master said, “any case in which a blemish…” [A note in the printed edition: it seems one should read that from this verse we do not learn about birds; but nonetheless an animal that copulated and one worshipped are disqualified among birds too, as in Ḥullin 23 and Zevaḥim 85a.]
rashi:b18.1: Filthy: that gives off sweat and smells foul.
rashi:b19.1: From the sheep, etc.: another verse: “And if his offering be of the flock, of the sheep or of the goats, for a burnt offering.”
gershom:b17.1: From the sheep, from the goats: with the vav of “and from the goats,” these are three exclusions.
gershom:b18.1: It is the manner of the verse to speak so: and they do not come for exposition. [The set-aside for idol worship is forbidden for the altar, and the coating on it is permitted for benefit, since it has not yet been worshipped. And both this and that, both the set-aside and the worshipped animal, are permitted for eating.]
rashi:b20.1: For seven years: that was set aside for seven years, and at the end of seven years they would sacrifice it to idol worship; for this is what set-aside is.
gershom:b19.1: The set-aside is forbidden for the altar only [if] it is one that has passed seven years since they set it aside for idol worship.
rashi:b21.1: And the bullock of seven years: that they fattened for seven years. Evidently that is their way of doing it.
gershom:b20.1: As it is stated: “And it came to pass that night, that the Lord said to him: Take your father’s bullock, and the second bullock of seven years”: this “second” [sheni] means fattened for seven years for idol worship, as in “and the cattle and the fatlings [mishnim].”
rashi:b22.1: It was also worshipped: I do not know where this is derived from.
rashi:b22.2: Another version: the prohibition of set-aside applies only for seven years, and from seven years on it is not set-aside, since they no longer sacrifice it, as it is written: “and the second bullock of seven years.” Evidently, because seven years had passed over it, it became permitted.
gershom:b21.1: And this one was only set-aside? But it was also worshipped, for it is called Baal, as it is written: “and throw down the altar of Baal,” [the altar] made for that bull, which is a Baal.
rashi:b22.3: Actually, they worshipped it: but we learn nothing from that case, since it is a novelty.
rashi:b22.5: And at night he sacrificed: for so it is written: “he did it by night.”
gershom:b22.1: And that whole deed of Gideon is a novelty: for it was outside, [and it was night,] which is not a time for sacrifice; and by a non-priest, since he was not a priest; and service vessels [the printed edition suggests: that were not consecrated as service vessels]; and the vessels of the asheira: they were of the asheira’s vessels.
